title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1RC0RF_1RD0LB_1RE0LD_1LF---_0RA1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1RC0RF_1RD0LB_1RE0LD_1LF---_0RA1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and it is a Collatz-like one. The first level of the run is decoded (the period rule is proved in Lean, the resets are measured). When the tail the resets feed on runs out it is rebuilt, and on the second level there are remainder classes that halt, classes that loop forever and classes that build a third level, all checked by direct simulation. Which one the real run meets is decided after about 10770 phases by the last digit of a number that triples every phase.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 62,434 cells have been visited and 38,014 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The turns at the left end, for every block length
claims.text: 0^inf (1100)^(n+1) C> 11 R and 0^inf 1 (1001)^(n+1) A> 1 R both reach 0^inf 1 (1001)^(n+1) 1001 B> R (16n+32 and 16n+33 steps): the head crosses the c block leftwards, bounces and crosses it back. From 0^inf A> 0 (1100)^(n+1) R it reaches 0^inf (1100)^(n+1) 1 B> R in 6n+7 steps. For all n and every tape R.

claims.title: A period, and a phase of periods, for every size
claims.text: 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^n (10110110)^(m+5) R reaches 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^(n+31) (10110110)^m R in 448n + 6952 steps, for all n, m and every tape R (it is never read); by induction, q periods take (n, m + 5q) to (n + 31q, m).

claims.title: An accelerated simulator, checked against the machine
claims.text: c/m7fast.c runs the machine and applies the period rule in one stroke wherever the tape has that form, with the exact step count. With VAL=11 it runs the plain machine beside it and compares the whole tape and state at 1,164 checkpoints (every jump and every record on the left in between) up to 5.9·1010 steps: no difference.

claims.title: The run to 4.5·10<sup>17</sup> steps
claims.text: From blank tape the phase ends (n, r) are (72, 0), (227, 0), (692, 2), (2,180, 2) and (6,799, 1) with the tail 1001; the resets give the new phases m = 35, 112, 352, 1,096 (n = 10). The reset of (6,799, 1), at step 373,111,704, writes the tail 10 (1110)^6805 1. After that the phase ends are (17, 0, 6805), (72, 1, 6801), (84, 0, 6800), (258, 4, 6796), ..., the last one followed being (235,599,917, 3, 6746) at step 447,668,812,972,368,258. No halt; the tape needed is then about 109 cells.

claims.where: py/m7map.py; c/m7fast.c 7 N R T for the constructed tapes

claims.title: 2,176 more phases without a halt
claims.text: Taking the table to hold for all n (it was measured for n up to 300 and matches the run up to n = 2.4·108), the map runs 2,176 more phases, to about 101541 steps and n of about 10770, without a halt, until t falls below 6. With t this small the constructed tapes show other resets, which rebuild a tail of about n words followed by a new suffix (1001101011001): a second level of the same kind, beyond any simulation.

claims.title: With a nearly empty second-level tail, one remainder class halts
claims.text: From 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^n (10110110)^2 10 (1110)^2 1001101011001 the machine halts, for every n tried (60 to 69, 80, 101; 31,436 steps at n = 60). The class is reachable from larger tails: with six words 1110 left, r = 0 and n ≡ 0 or 9 (mod 10), the next phase ends in it and halts (n = 60, 69, 160, 1009 checked by direct simulation). With the first-level tail (ending in a single 1) no class with 0 to 7 words left halts.

claims.title: Other classes loop forever or rebuild the tail
claims.text: With an empty or nearly empty tail the other classes either enter a loop that adds five words 1100 per round without end (seen for 3,000 rounds; for example r = 1 with the tail 101), or rebuild a tail of about 3.1 n words 1110 with the suffix 1001101011001, or reach a short tail (1, 1001, 1011101). The tables list every class with 0 to 7 words left for both tails, n = 60 to 69.

claims.title: Where the real run stands
claims.text: Iterating the reset table (measured, not proved, for all n) the first level ends after 2,176 more phases at r = 3 with three words left and n ≡ 11 (mod 100), a number of 771 digits. For n ≡ 1 (mod 10) that reset builds the second-level tail with 31(n−1)/10 + 92 words (checked for n = 61 to 211). The second level then lasts about 10<sup>770</sup> phases, n roughly tripling in each, and how it ends (halt, loop or a third level) depends on n mod 10 and r at that moment, which nobody can compute. So the closed-set method does not apply: a halting class is reachable, and this is a Collatz-like question.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The only halting transition is E reading 1. The first level (periods and the reset table) is decoded with exact step counts and never halts while the tail lasts; the question moves to the resets at a nearly empty tail, which start a next level whose numbers have hundreds of digits.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine keeps two blocks of words side by side: one grows while the other shrinks, and when the second is used up the first is turned into it, about three times larger than last time.

facts.text: One period trades five d words for 31 c words; proved in Lean for every size.
Followed exactly, jumping over the periods, without a halt.
Where the exact reset table, iterated, runs out of tail.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.561). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 62,434 cells (48,420 left of the start, 45 right), with a density of 1s of 0.609.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Two blocks of words
html:
Left of the start the tape reads

0^inf c^n J d^m 1 0 (1110)^r ...

with c = 1100, d = 10110110 and a short junction J. The head shuttles between the left end and J; the bounces at the left end are proved in Lean. J cycles through a few shapes, and over the cycle the c block gains about 6.2 words for each d word it eats.

sections.heading: When the d's run out
html:
A period of 84 trips to the left end trades five d's for 31 c's; Lean proves this for every size and whatever lies further right. When fewer than five d's are left the phase ends with a remainder r, and a reset follows. From step 3.7·108 on, the tail right of the d's is a run of t words 1110, and the resets follow an exact table:

rnexttsteps
0new phase, m′ = ⌈(n+4)/2⌉t−4151n + 1560 (n even), 151n + 1605 (odd)
1(n+12, 0)t−1192n + 1374
2(n+32, 0)t−4512n + 8840
3new phase, m′ = ⌊(n+25)/2⌋t−3471n + 8170 (even), 471n + 8215 (odd)
4new phase, m′ = ⌊(n+26)/2⌋t−2471n + 8286 (even), 471n + 8241 (odd)

A new phase starts with n = 10 and m′ d's and ends after ⌊m′/5⌋ periods. So n roughly triples from phase to phase while t shrinks by one to four words. The table reproduces every phase end of the run to 4.5·1017 steps; iterated on its own it lasts 2,176 more phases, until t is almost used up, and then a different reset builds a much longer tail: the same structure one level up.

sections.heading: Some remainder classes halt, some loop
html: A method that settled another holdout keeps the big counts free and follows only small remainders; it proves non-halting when no remainder class can halt. Here it finds the opposite. Leave the number n of words 1100 free and try every remainder r and every nearly empty tail:

tail after the two blocksrwhat happens (every n tried)
10 (1110)^2 10011010110012halts (31,436 steps at n = 60)
10 (1110)^6 10011010110010halts if n ends in 0 or 9; otherwise goes on
10 11loops forever, five more words 1100 per round
10 (1110)^3 13n ending in 1: rebuilds a tail of 31(n−1)/10 + 92 words (the real run's case)

So the machine can halt, can loop forever, or can start a third level, depending on a last digit after about 10770 phases in which n triples each time. That is the same kind of question as the Collatz problem, and no proof either way is in sight.

family: two blocks trading words, with resets (nested; a halting class exists on the second level)
summary: Two blocks trade words (31 for 5, proved in Lean) with resets that depend on a remainder mod 5; the tail that the resets consume is rebuilt once it runs out, and on the second level some remainder classes halt and others loop forever, so the outcome turns on a Collatz-like question about a number with about 10^770 digits of phases.
